subject: Vocabulary
topic: Difficult Vocabulary — Meanings of Advanced SSC Words (W11 B2)

options.option_text: A person who is excessively flattering to gain favour
A person who studies ancient languages
A person who is skilled in diplomacy
A person who challenges authority

questions.explanation: A is correct. SYCOPHANT = a person who acts obsequiously towards someone powerful to gain advantage; a flatterer or 'yes-man'. Example: 'He surrounded himself with sycophants who never challenged his decisions.' Root: Greek 'sykophantes' (informer). Synonyms: toady, flatterer, bootlicker. Trap: 'skilled in diplomacy' = diplomat; 'challenges authority' = insurgent/rebel (opposite of a sycophant).

options.option_text: Prone to begging
Not telling the truth; lying
Skilled in negotiation
Relating to the mind

questions.explanation: B is correct. MENDACIOUS = not telling the truth; dishonest. The noun is MENDACITY (habitual lying). Example: 'The mendacious politician made promises he never intended to keep.' Root: Latin 'mendax' = lying. Trap: 'prone to begging' = mendicant (sounds similar — MENDICANT ≠ MENDACIOUS); 'relating to the mind' = mental/cerebral.

options.option_text: Stubbornly refusing to change opinion
Excessively eager to serve or please
Full of careful thought and planning
Having strong moral principles

questions.explanation: B is correct. OBSEQUIOUS = obedient or attentive to an excessive or servile degree; fawning, subservient. Example: 'The obsequious assistant agreed with every word the boss said.' Root: Latin 'obsequi' = to comply. Synonyms: servile, subservient, sycophantic. Trap: 'stubbornly refusing' = obstinate (sounds similar but opposite meaning); 'strong moral principles' = righteous.

options.option_text: A sharp, harsh, or bitter quality in manner or speech
A feeling of great happiness
A ceremony marking an important event
A sharp flavour in food

questions.explanation: A is correct. ACRIMONY = bitterness or ill feeling (especially in communication). The adjective is ACRIMONIOUS. Example: 'The divorce proceedings were marked by acrimony and bitter recriminations.' Root: Latin 'acrimonia' = sharpness. Trap: 'a sharp flavour' = the word 'acrid' relates to sharp taste/smell (different word); 'great happiness' = elation/euphoria (opposite sentiment).

options.option_text: Done with great care and attention
Carried out with minimal effort; done merely as a routine
Performed with great enthusiasm
Completed before the deadline

questions.explanation: B is correct. PERFUNCTORY = carried out with minimal effort and care, done merely as a routine duty; lacking interest or effort. Example: 'He gave a perfunctory glance at the report and signed it without reading properly.' Root: Latin 'perfungi' = to get through with. Trap: 'great care and attention' = meticulous/thorough (antonym); 'great enthusiasm' = zealous (antonym of perfunctory).

options.option_text: Obedient and cooperative
Having an ability to recover quickly
Stubbornly uncooperative; resistant to authority
Easily persuaded to change one's mind

questions.explanation: C is correct. RECALCITRANT = having an obstinately uncooperative attitude; resisting authority or control. Example: 'The recalcitrant prisoner refused to follow any of the prison's rules.' Root: Latin 'recalcitrare' = to kick back. Trap: 'ability to recover quickly' = resilient/RESILIENT (sounds somewhat similar); 'obedient and cooperative' = compliant (antonym).

options.option_text: Mental calmness, especially in difficult situations
Equal treatment of all people
A feeling of intense excitement
The quality of being equal in value

questions.explanation: A is correct. EQUANIMITY = calmness and composure, especially in difficult situations; mental tranquility. Example: 'She faced the crisis with remarkable equanimity, never losing her composure.' Root: Latin 'aequus' (equal) + 'animus' (mind) = an even or balanced mind. Trap: 'equal treatment' = equity/equality; 'equal in value' = equivalence — these share the 'equi' root but have entirely different meanings.

options.option_text: To invest money in a capital city
To summarise the main points of an argument
To cease resisting; to give in to an opponent
To execute a criminal by decapitation

questions.explanation: C is correct. CAPITULATE = to cease resisting an opponent and submit; to surrender. Example: 'After weeks of protest, the government capitulated and withdrew the unpopular bill.' Root: Latin 'capitulare' = to draw up under headings (terms of surrender). Trap: 'summarise main points' = RECAPITULATE (a related but different word, meaning 'to summarise'); 'decapitation' shares the Latin 'caput' (head) root but is an entirely different word.

options.option_text: To waver indecisively between different opinions
To speak loudly and at great length
To travel rapidly from place to place
To make empty or hollow

questions.explanation: A is correct. VACILLATE = to alternate or waver between different opinions or actions; to be indecisive. Example: 'He vacillated between accepting the offer and staying in his current job.' Root: Latin 'vacillare' = to sway. Synonyms: dither, waver, oscillate. Trap: 'make empty or hollow' = vacate/evacuate (shares the Latin root 'vacuus' = empty, but different meaning); 'speak loudly' = declaim/orate.

options.option_text: Having a helpful and positive influence
Having a harmful effect, especially in a gradual way
Relating to the study of crime
Being extremely stubborn and inflexible

questions.explanation: B is correct. PERNICIOUS = having a harmful effect, especially one that is gradual or not immediately obvious; destructive. Example: 'The pernicious influence of misinformation is slowly eroding public trust.' Root: Latin 'perniciosus' = destructive (pernicies = destruction). Synonyms: harmful, injurious, deleterious, baneful. Trap: 'helpful and positive' = beneficial (antonym); 'study of crime' = criminology (unrelated); 'stubborn' = obstinate (unrelated).
